extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of philosophy (Kantian aesthetics and teleology); readers of Critique of Judgement
extracted.subtask_description: Principles and criteria for judging purposiveness in nature (distinguishing intellectual, empirical, and internal purposiveness) and for identifying organised beings as natural purposes; regulative maxims for teleological reflection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intellectual purposiveness (mathematical objects)
rubrics_metrics.description: An intellectual purposiveness is objective (not merely subjective like aesthetical purposiveness) but merely formal (not real); it can be conceived as purposiveness in general without any definite purpose being assumed as its basis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: properties of the circle, parabola, ellipse discovered a priori by geometer’s concepts—these show purposiveness for cognitive uses although no empirical purpose is involved. Such satisfaction is called 'relative perfection' rather than beauty of the mathematical figure; demonstrations of these properties are 'beautiful' or 'elegant' because they strengthen Understanding and Imagination a priori.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between empirical (external) purposiveness and formal (a priori) purposiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: Order and regularity found in complexes of things external to ourselves (e.g., a garden) are empirical and must be given experience to be known, whereas forms like geometric figures are determined a priori in our representation and are not empirical purposiveness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical purposiveness (real) depends on the concept of a purpose and cannot be derived a priori from the form of our intuition; formal purposiveness (as in mathematical figures) does not imply any actual purpose in objects themselves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relative purposiveness (utility) vs inner purposiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: Relative purposiveness (utility or mere advantage) is purposiveness of something as a means to other beings' ends; inner purposiveness is when a natural being's form is purposive for itself (an 'inner' purpose).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of relative purposiveness: rivers depositing earth useful for plant growth, sand enabling pine forests, snow protecting crops or enabling sleigh travel. These are only hypothetically purposive (advantageous) and do not on their own justify absolute teleological judgements about nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion: thing possible only as a purpose (contingency of form)
rubrics_metrics.description: A thing is to be regarded as only possible as a purpose when its form is not possible according to mere natural laws (i.e., empirical knowledge of it presupposes concepts of Reason); the contingency of its form relative to natural laws suggests causality by Reason.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: discovering a regular hexagon on sand would incline one to attribute it to an artful cause (Reason) rather than to mechanical natural causes because chance of such a form arising mechanically seems infinitely improbable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of organised product of nature (principle of internal purposiveness)
rubrics_metrics.description: An organised product of nature is one in which every part is reciprocally purpose [end] and means; in it nothing is vain, without purpose, or to be ascribed to a blind mechanism of nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This principle is a maxim for judging internal purposiveness: it guides observation and morphological inquiry (e.g., dissectors assume nothing in a creature is vain) and while derived from experience it functions as an a priori regulative principle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Condition: parts possible only through reference to the whole
rubrics_metrics.description: For a natural product to be thought as a natural purpose its parts (in being and form) must be possible only through reference to the whole; the whole (Idea) must a priori determine what is to be contained in it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If parts are determined by an externally imposed Idea, the product would be an artificial work; in natural purposes the unity of the whole is internally manifested by the dependence of parts on that whole.

rubrics_metrics.name: Condition: reciprocal causality of parts (parts as cause and effect of one another)
rubrics_metrics.description: The parts of an organised being must so combine that they are reciprocally cause and effect of each other's form, enabling the Idea of the whole to determine the form and combination of all parts (not as an external cause but as ground of cognition).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This mutual dependence distinguishes organised natural products from artificial instruments: in organisms each part exists by means of the others and for the sake of the others and the whole (organs reciprocally producing each other).

rubrics_metrics.name: Organised beings are self-organising (formative power vs mere mechanism)
rubrics_metrics.description: Organised beings possess formative power of a self-propagating kind, communicating formative activity to their materials (which do not have it themselves); they organise and can maintain, reproduce, or repair themselves in ways mere mechanical objects cannot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrast with a watch: watch-parts move and serve ends but do not produce or repair one another, nor does a watch replace missing parts by organising foreign material; organised nature does all this (growth, regeneration, self-maintenance).

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion: thing as both cause and effect of itself (self-production in two senses)
rubrics_metrics.description: A thing exists as a natural purpose if it is both cause and effect of itself: (1) generically (a tree produces trees of its genus) and (2) individually (growth where the organism makes specific form out of material not itself able to produce that form).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: trees generate others of the same genus and grow by transforming educts into organised parts; parts may be able to engraft and produce like parts, and organisms can respond to injury by self-help (regeneration), illustrating self-propagating causality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teleological judging of nature in general: regulative maxim ('nothing is vain')
rubrics_metrics.description: As a regulative maxim for reflective judgement, we may assume that everything in the world is somehow good for something, that nothing is vain in it; this guides investigation of natural phenomena under the idea of nature as a system of purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is not a constitutive principle (it does not assert that nature is literally designed) but a heuristic for inquiry: it legitimizes seeking final-cause explanations in biology while remaining compatible with mechanical causality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitation: external purposiveness insufficient to justify final purpose of nature
rubrics_metrics.description: External or relative purposiveness (things advantageous to other beings) does not justify regarding those things as final purposes of nature; to assert a final purpose of nature requires knowledge that transcends empirical teleological judgement (a reference to the supersensible).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: grass useful for oxen or oxen useful for humans do not show that men must exist as a final purpose; attributing a final purpose to nature requires assuming something beyond mere physical-teleological observation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodological distinction: teleological judging is reflective and regulative, not determinant or constitutive
rubrics_metrics.description: Teleological principles serve as regulative maxims for reflective judgement to guide investigation of organised natural products; they do not constitute objective constitutive laws of nature but orient our inquiry into possible final-causes alongside mechanical explanations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use teleological judgement to form hypotheses and direct observation (e.g., considering organs as purposive aids morphological study), but do not mistake this method for proving nature is designed or for supplanting mechanistic causality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aesthetic notions vs intellectual purposiveness: admiration, wonder, and relative perfection
rubrics_metrics.description: Wonder is the shock from incompatibility of a representation with its underlying principles; admiration is recurring wonder and arises from observed purposiveness of things. Mathematical 'beauty' is better described as 'relative perfection' grounded in intellectual purposiveness, not the free play of the faculties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish aesthetic (free play) judgements of beauty from intellectual satisfaction in discovering necessary synthetical rules; call demonstrations 'beautiful' or 'elegant' when they exhibit such intellectual purposiveness.
